title: How do you cache content that's personalized per user?
summary: Tests whether you know techniques beyond "you can't cache personalized data" — per-user keys, fragment caching, and caching the expensive shared part separately from the cheap personal part.

slides.markdown:
"Personalized means uncacheable" is a myth the interviewer wants you to push past. Personalization doesn't make caching impossible — it makes the naive, page-level version of caching wrong. The real technique is to **split the response**: cache the expensive, shared part normally, and handle the cheap, personal part separately.

The strong answer names concrete techniques — per-user cache keys, fragment caching — instead of stopping at "you can't cache this."

Ask: **which part of the response is actually personalized, and which part is shared across users?** A page or API response rarely is 100% personalized end to end — usually there's an expensive, largely-shared computation (a ranking, a recommendation set) mixed with a cheap, genuinely per-user detail (a "liked by your friend" annotation).

Misjudging this split is the root cause of both failure modes covered later: caching nothing wastes the shared part's savings, and caching everything wastes memory on the cheap part.

State the rule: **split the response — cache the shared, expensive part normally; cache the personal, cheap part per-user or not at all.** "Expensive" and "shared" tend to travel together (a ranking model's output is costly to compute and largely the same computation across users), while "cheap" and "personal" tend to travel together (an annotation that's fast to compute live and inherently different per user).

Caching decisions should follow that pairing, not the label "personalized" alone.

slides.sectionTitle: Worked example: a feed's ranking output vs its social annotation
slides.markdown:
| | Ranking model output | "Liked by 3 friends" annotation |
|---|---|---|
| Cost to compute | Expensive — a model inference over the user's graph and history | Cheap — a small lookup against recent likes |
| Personalization | Per-user, but the expensive part is worth caching anyway | Genuinely tiny and per-user |
| Right approach | Cache per-user with a short TTL — expensive enough to be worth it even scoped to one user | Compute live on every request |

**How to decide:** cache per-user when the compute cost saved is worth the memory cost of a per-user copy; compute live when the cost is already negligible, since caching it saves almost nothing and still costs memory.

slides.sectionTitle: Per-user cache keys and the memory-multiplication cost
slides.markdown:
Per-user caching means the cache key includes the user ID — `feed-ranking:user:42` instead of a single shared key — which means the memory cost is **N users × the cached payload size**, not one payload's worth. A ranking result that's 2KB per user, cached for 10 million active users, is 20GB of cache memory just for that one cached artifact.

This is the number that should drive the decision on *whether* to cache per-user at all, not just *how*.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: fragment caching a page with a personalized widget
slides.markdown:
![Shared page shell cached at the CDN with a personalized widget stitched in per request](assets/shell-vs-personalized.svg)

The page shell — navigation, layout, static content — is shared and cached normally, often at the CDN. The personalized widget is fetched separately, per request, and stitched into the response at the edge or in the app layer.

This is the concrete mechanism behind "split the response": the shell never varies per user and gets full caching benefit; the personalized piece never gets cached at all, and that's fine because it's the cheap part.

assets.alt: Shared page shell cached at the CDN with a personalized widget stitched in per request

slides.sectionTitle: The trade-off to name out loud
slides.markdown:
| Caching per-user | Computing live |
|---|---|
| Cuts compute cost on every repeat request | No cache memory cost at all |
| Memory cost multiplies by user count | Compute cost paid every single time |

**How to decide:** per-user caching only pays off when recomputing is genuinely expensive — if a ranking model inference costs real CPU time and money, caching it per-user for a short TTL is worth the memory. If the underlying computation is already cheap, the memory cost of caching it per-user isn't worth paying for near-zero savings.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: "the personalization model changes — how do you invalidate millions of per-user entries?"
slides.markdown:
You don't invalidate millions of individual keys one at a time — you **version the cache key itself**: include a model version in the key (`feed-ranking:v7:user:42`), and when the model updates to v8, every lookup for a v7 key simply misses and recomputes fresh under the new version. The old v7 entries age out via TTL naturally, with zero explicit deletion required.

This sidesteps a mass-invalidation problem entirely by making the old entries irrelevant rather than trying to delete them all.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: "would you rather recompute cheaply or cache expensively here?"
slides.markdown:
Do the arithmetic rather than guessing: compare the **compute cost saved per cache hit** against the **memory cost of holding one entry per user**. If a computation costs 50ms of CPU and the result is 2KB, caching it for an hour at a high hit rate saves a lot of CPU for a modest memory spend. If the computation is 2ms and the result is 50KB, the trade flips — you're paying a lot of memory to save very little compute.

Stating this as a ratio you'd actually estimate, rather than a gut call, is what a senior answer sounds like here.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: the two opposite overreactions to "it's personalized"
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief (overreaction one):** "It's personalized, so we can't cache any of it." **Wrong belief (overreaction two):** "It's personalized, so we'll cache the entire response per user."

**Why both are wrong:** the first throws away real savings on the shared, expensive part of the response; the second blows up memory by caching the cheap, per-user part too, multiplying cost for almost no benefit.

**Correct model:** split the response by cost and shareability, not by the single label "personalized" — cache what's expensive and shared normally, cache what's expensive and per-user with a per-user key, and compute what's cheap live regardless of whose data it is.

Personalized doesn't mean uncacheable — split the response into its shared/expensive part (cache normally, or per-user if expensive enough to justify it) and its cheap/personal part (compute live). Per-user caching costs N users × payload size in memory, so only do it when the compute savings justify that. Version cache keys by model version to sidestep mass invalidation when personalization logic changes. Fragment/edge-include caching is the concrete mechanism for splitting a page between a shared shell and a live personalized piece.
